tutorial.title: Around the World - Part 2
tutorial.descriptionContent: In the second part, you'll set up the front-end to consume the API and display a loaded airport on a map

executableContent.instructions:
Welcome back to the **Around the World** project. In part 2, we'll work on the front-end that will consume the API we built in the first part.

We're starting with a simple React template.

Additionally, we hosted the back-end at `https://airports.mimo.dev` so we can actually use the built API endpoints. The endpoint that we built together in part one is ready to be used.

Let's get familiar with the React template and make a first tiny change.

1. Change the title of the React app to `Around the World` in `index.html`.

executableContent.instructions:
Let's fetch a random airport from our API now.

1. In `App.jsx`, create an async function named `loadRandomAirport()`.
2. Inside it, fetch a random airport from `https://airports.mimo.dev/api/random-airport`.
3. Convert the response to JSON, and save it in a variable called `data`. We'll use that in a minute.
4. Add a `useEffect` that calls `loadRandomAirport()`. Ensure to import `useEffect` to be able to use the hook. 
5. Make sure the dependency array is `[]` so it only runs once.

executableContent.instructions:
Next, we'll display a map to soon show the airport we load from our API. We'll use Leaflet for the map.

Add the Leaflet CSS and JavaScript files to the `<head>` of the `index.html` file. We'll also prepare some CSS that we'll need.

This won't show the map yet, but it sets everything up.

1. Add a `<link>` element for the Leaflet stylesheet in the `<head>` element to load the necessary code into our project.
   ```HTML
   <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.css"/>
   ```
2. Add a `<script>` element for the Leaflet JavaScript file in the `<head>` element.
   ```HTML
   <script src="https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.js"></script>
   ```
3. In `App.css`, set the `height` to `40vh` and the `margin` to `20px` for `.map`.

executableContent.instructions:
Next, we’ll create the component to display the map. We are going to use a map system called Leaflet. It's similar to other maps, such as Google Maps or Apple Maps. 

It uses a little bit of funky syntax at times, but for now, just go with it. 

1. In `AirportMap.jsx`, import `React` and `useEffect`.
2. Create an `AirportMap` functional component.
3. Create an `useEffect` hook, create a Leaflet map insight the `useEffect` block, and set the viewport:
   ```JavaScript
   const L = window.L;
   const map = L.map("map").setView([0, 0], 2);
   ```
4. Still inside the `useEffect` block, add the OpenStreetMap tile layer to the map:
   ```JavaScript
   L.tileLayer("https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png").addTo(map);
   ```
5. Add a cleanup function that removes the map when the component unmounts at the end of the `useEffect` block:
   ```JavaScript
   return () => map.remove();
   ```
6. After the `useEffect`, return a `<div>` element with the id `map` and the class `map`:
7. Export `AirportMap` as the default export.
8. Heading over to `App.jsx`, import `AirportMap` and render it.

executableContent.instructions:
Now, we'll display the passed airport on the rendered map.

1. In `AirportMap`, at the beginning of the `useEffect` hook, check whether `airport` is available. Return early when it is not
2. Create a `position` array using the airport’s `latitude_deg` and `longitude_deg` properties:
   ```javascript
   const position = [airport.latitude_deg, airport.longitude_deg];
   ```
3. Set the map view to `position` instead of the generic `[0, 0]` coordinates and keep the margin of `2`. 
4. Add a marker at the airport’s position and add it to the map:
   ```javascript
   L.marker(position).addTo(map);
   ```
5. Add `airport` to the `useEffect` dependency array to run that piece of code whenever the past variable `airport` changes.
